name: Revenge
label: Factory Records
lede: When New Order stalled in 1989, Peter Hook went to his own studio in Rochdale, took the lead vocal and made a dance-rock record with a glamour photographer's shot on the sleeve.

eras.title: Hook takes the mic
eras.text: New Order had stopped working as a band, and Peter Hook had a studio of his own. He built Revenge out of the people already in the building: the house engineer, a local guitarist and the teenage tape operator.

years.big: "Fuck it, I'll do my own thing."
years.h: Sumner says he's out, in a Los Angeles hotel room
years.p: Hook's account of the meeting where [[Bernard Sumner|6fa2e161-200e-475a-8492-3755594581f9]] told New Order he was leaving. Sumner went on to form [[Electronic|3cdb360e-d0a2-459f-92f6-f0f28e62127d]] with [[Johnny Marr|ff621094-2a76-401f-8398-b75b5fd2be24]]; Hook went to his studio in Rochdale.
years.xp: "I was completely bewildered," Hook told LTM of the meeting. New Order's own line at the time was gentler. "The whole idea of New Order taking this time off was planned long ago," he told an American interviewer in 1990.

years.cap: Peter Hook at Revenge's first gig, the Skin Two party, Town & Country Club, London, from NME
years.h: Suite 16's engineer and a Lavolta Lakota guitarist join Hook
years.p: Hook co-owned Suite 16 in Rochdale with Shan Hira of [[Stockholm Monsters|e1033f2d-04db-4fd8-827a-fbb2ef07a11d]]. House engineer Chris "C.J." Jones took keyboards, Dave Hicks came over from Lavolta Lakota, and tape op David "Pottsy" Potts and drummer Ash Major filled out the live band.
years.xp:
Hook sang and played bass, and the songs were credited to the trio. "To say this is a solo project is to demean it," he said in 1990.

The working chemistry took time. "If I wasn't around, they stopped working," Hook told LTM of Jones and Hicks.

years.h: 7 Reasons is FAC 247, and Revenge's first record
years.p: A 12-inch and CD single on Factory Records, with "Jesus... I Love You" on the flip and an instrumental called "I Love You Too".

eras.title: Big in American clubs
eras.text: Factory put Revenge out at home and Capitol took it to North America, where "Pineapple Face" got further up the charts than anything on the British side. The band toured the US in the summer and Germany in the autumn.

years.h: "Pineapple Face" hits No. 8 on US Modern Rock
years.p: FAC 267 in Britain, Capitol in North America. It also reached No. 10 on Billboard's club play chart.
years.xp: One remix came from Ron St. Germain, who had engineered for [[Jimi Hendrix|06fb1c8b-566e-4cb2-985b-b467c90781d4]]. LTM says the video, Hook with a cast of women and a twist at the end, was held back by broadcasters.

years.cap: Dave Hicks, Chris Jones and Peter Hook in the US press photo for One True Passion, 1990
years.src: Cerysmatic: FACT 230 · LTM: Revenge · World in Motion
years.h: One True Passion, with a Suze Randall photo on the front
years.p: [[Peter Saville|e61408b0-767c-4dde-ad88-a052456efcfe]] art-directed the sleeve around a shot by glamour photographer Suze Randall. Revenge produced it at Suite 16, and Alan Meyerson mixed it at Larrabee in Los Angeles.
years.xp:
Eight songs, from "Pineapple Face" to the closer "It's Quiet". Hook later said he'd overloaded the tracks: "I couldn't bear to throw anything away." He also thought the songs played better on stage than on the record.

Writing the words was the hard part. He wrote the vocal first only on "It's Quiet" and "14K", and rated himself "a 6 1/2 or 7 out of 10" as a lyricist.

years.h: A North American tour, then a long run across Germany
years.p: Hook said later that Revenge "took us everywhere around the world" and still came out ahead: it didn't lose money.

years.h: "Slave" comes with a John Cale cover on the B-side
years.p: FAC 279 pairs remixes of the album track with Revenge's version of [[John Cale|72c090b6-a68e-4cb9-b330-85278681a714]]'s "Amsterdam". A third single, "Kiss the Chrome", was planned and dropped.

eras.title: A new five-piece, then New Order calls
eras.text: Hicks left, Potts moved to guitar and a new rhythm section came in. The five-piece played Manchester's big Factory weekend and made one more record before New Order started up again.

years.h: Revenge covers "White Light/White Heat" for a Velvets tribute
years.p: The track went onto the [[The Velvet Underground|Velvet Underground]] tribute album Heaven and Hell, and became an encore at some shows.

years.h: Hicks leaves, Potts moves to guitar, two new players arrive
years.p: Dave Hicks wanted to sing lead, and drummer Ash Major quit with an injury. Brian Whittaker took bass and Mike Hedges took the drums.
years.xp:
By Hook's account to LTM, Hicks would take tracks home, put his own vocals on them and play them to people before Hook heard them. "C.J. and I found it easier to work with Pottsy than with Dave," Hook said.

Potts switching from bass changed Hook too. "When I had Revenge, I was really wound up about sounding like New Order," he said. "Pottsy helped me to dispel it."

years.cap: Advert for Cities in the Park, Heaton Park, August 3-4, 1991
years.src: LTM: Revenge · Wikipedia: Cities in the Park · Concert Archives
years.h: Revenge plays the Martin Hannett tribute in Heaton Park
years.p: Cities in the Park in Heaton Park, Manchester, honoured producer [[Martin Hannett|ffbfce58-5185-4bcc-8c45-a7cd5d1a3783]], who had died that April. Revenge played new songs "State of Shock" and "Cloud 9" and ended on "Dreams Never End", the New Order song Hook had sung on Movement.
years.xp: [[Happy Mondays|01f4fb92-6bf0-4de5-83dc-3fe194e763bf]], [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]] and Sumner's [[Electronic|3cdb360e-d0a2-459f-92f6-f0f28e62127d]] were on the Factory bill the same Sunday, so both halves of New Order's split played the same field.

years.h: Gun World Porn, the last Revenge record
years.p: A mini-album, FACD 327, built around "Little Pig", "Deadbeat", "Cloud 9" and "State of Shock". Hook said it tells "how confused I was, really".

years.cap: Chris Jones and David Potts at Revenge rehearsals in New Order's Cheetham Hill rehearsal room, Manchester, 1992
years.h: New Order starts again and Revenge comes apart
years.p: Hook couldn't keep a five-piece going around New Order's schedule. Everyone drifted off except Potts.
years.xp: Hook took one lesson from it: his home life mattered as much as the band, "whereas in New Order, we always put the band in front of our home lives."

eras.title: Monaco, and the vault opens
eras.text: Hook and Potts came back as a duo with a different sound. A decade after the split, LTM put the Revenge catalogue back out with unfinished songs completed by New Order's own crew.

years.p: Their single "What Do You Want From Me?" became a UK hit.

years.src: LTM: Revenge · LTM: One True Passion V2.0
years.p: LTM's reissue (LTMCD 2375) comes with a bonus CD, Be Careful What You Wish For, including two songs from the last shows, "The Wilding" and "Televive", finished for the set.
years.xp: Hook finished them with New Order guitarist [[Phil Cunningham|d3f20658-d306-4fb0-9a80-7b455994f2c4]] and programmer Roger Lyons. "The tracks sound great. I'm really pleased with them," he said.

years.h: No Pain No Gain captures the 1991 five-piece live
years.p: LTM's live album (LTMCD 2413) is the line-up with Potts on guitar, Whittaker on bass and Hedges on drums.

sources.title: Concert Archives: Cities in the Park, Aug 4 1991
